set1.q: A 54-year-old woman who has taken opioid medications for chronic back pain for years has snoring, frequent awakenings and daytime sleepiness. Which sleep study fits her?
opts: Home kits assess obstructive sleep apnea and not other sleep disorders. Tell: her years of opioid use raise the possibility of central apnea and place her on the list of patients who need a polysomnogram instead.
ruled out by a stated finding

A questionnaire places a patient in a risk group and cannot diagnose; screening tools have value in symptomatic patients in high-risk settings such as preoperative evaluation. Tell: she already has symptoms, and opioid use decides which study she needs.
A titration study sets the device pressure once the diagnosis is known. Tell: she has no diagnosis yet, and her long-term opioid use points to a diagnostic polysomnogram first.

Correct. Long-term opioid use is one of the settings where a polysomnogram, not an at-home kit, is used. Opioid medications are also a risk factor for central sleep apnea, which home kits cannot assess, since they assess obstructive sleep apnea and not other sleep disorders.

set1.q: A 78-year-old woman with obstructive sleep apnea has residual daytime sleepiness despite continuous positive airway pressure, and armodafinil is being considered. She has no heart, liver or psychiatric disease. Which approach to its dose fits her?
opts: Avoiding the drug because of age
Older age calls for a lower dose, not for avoiding the drug. Tell: the conditions that call for caution are cardiovascular, hepatic and psychiatric disease, and she has none of them.
A lower dose than in younger adults

Correct. Stimulants such as modafinil and armodafinil are given at lower doses in the elderly population. At 78, with no cardiovascular, hepatic or psychiatric condition to add caution, she can be considered for the drug at a reduced dose.
A higher dose than in younger adults
Age moves the dose down, not up: lower doses are used in the elderly population. Tell: for a 78-year-old the stimulant caution is a lower dose, never a higher one.
The same dose as in younger adults
The elderly are singled out for lower doses, so the standard adult dose is not the plan for a 78-year-old. Tell: her age alone is enough to lower the stimulant dose.

set1.q: A 43-year-old woman with habitual snoring and daytime sleepiness has a home sleep apnea test that does not show obstructive sleep apnea. Her symptoms persist. What is the best next step?
opts: Stimulants such as modafinil treat sleepiness but carry headaches, anxiety and many drug interactions. Tell: she has no diagnosis yet, and treating the symptom would skip the study that could find mild disease.

Correct. At-home kits will not always diagnose mild obstructive sleep apnea; they are most helpful in moderate to severe disease. A negative home study in a woman with ongoing snoring and sleepiness therefore needs a polysomnogram, which can also find other sleep disorders a home kit cannot assess.
A negative home study does not exclude mild disease, since home kits will not always diagnose it. Tell: her symptoms persist, so the question stays open until a polysomnogram answers it.

Repeating the same kind of study repeats its limits: home kits assess obstructive sleep apnea alone and can miss mild disease. Tell: the polysomnogram is the study that measures severity across sleep stages and positions.

set1.q: A 57-year-old man with newly diagnosed obstructive sleep apnea drinks several glasses of wine each night and takes an over-the-counter sedative to fall asleep. Which advice addresses these modifiable risk factors?
opts: Keep the wine, stop the sedative

Stopping the sedative while keeping the wine leaves alcohol, itself a listed risk factor, in his nightly routine. Tell: risk modification names alcohol together with other sedatives, so the wine is part of the problem too.
Take both earlier in the evening

Changing the timing still leaves alcohol and a sedative in his routine, and the risk modification is to avoid them. Tell: the advice is avoidance of alcohol and other sedatives, not rescheduling them around bedtime.

Correct. Use of alcohol or sedatives is a risk factor for obstructive sleep apnea, and the risk modifications are to avoid alcohol and other sedatives, along with diet and exercise for weight loss. Both his nightly wine and his sleep aid fall under that advice.
Keep the sedative, stop the wine

Stopping the wine while keeping the sedative leaves one of the two named risk factors in place. Tell: the advice covers alcohol and other sedatives together, so the over-the-counter sleep aid has to go as well as the wine.

set1.q: A 62-year-old woman is diagnosed with obesity hypoventilation syndrome. She has coexisting obstructive sleep apnea, and her awake room-air oxygen saturation is 85% (normal 95-100%). Which feature of her presentation points to a poor prognosis?
opts: Patients may present in their 50s and 60s, so her age is typical, not a prognostic marker. Tell: the feature tied to poor prognosis is significant awake hypoxemia at diagnosis.

About 90% of patients have coexisting obstructive sleep apnea symptoms, so it is the usual picture, not a marker of a worse outcome. Tell: her awake saturation of 85% is the feature linked to poor prognosis.

Correct. Prognosis is poor when there is significant awake hypoxemia at diagnosis and with positive airway pressure therapy. Her awake room-air saturation of 85% is well below normal, and the syndrome already carries high mortality and morbidity, with cardiovascular disease the leading cause of death.

Sex is not the named prognostic marker: male gender is not even a risk factor for the syndrome, and older women make up the sleep-hypoventilation subgroup. Tell: the marker of poor prognosis is significant awake hypoxemia.

set1.q: A 64-year-old woman developed central sleep apnea after a stroke. She takes no opioids, has normal heart function and lives at sea level. Which therapy is considered first?
opts: Autotitrating positive airway pressure is an obstructive sleep apnea option for patients without significant comorbid conditions. Tell: the device named first for central sleep apnea is continuous positive airway pressure.

Correct. Treatment of central sleep apnea addresses an underlying cause (heart failure, opioids or altitude), and none applies to her. The next step is to consider continuous positive airway pressure first, with adaptive servo-ventilation held for when it fails.

Adaptive servo-ventilation is considered if continuous positive airway pressure fails, and it is not used for every patient because of safety concerns. Tell: she has not yet tried continuous pressure.

Bilevel positive airway pressure is the first-line device, with weight loss, for obesity hypoventilation syndrome with sleep-related hypoventilation. Tell: for central sleep apnea, the device considered first is continuous positive airway pressure.

set1.q: A 46-year-old woman feels tired and sleepy most days, and her husband has seen her stop breathing and gasp during sleep. She does not snore loudly and is not treated for high blood pressure. Her body mass index is 37 kg/m2 and her neck (shirt collar) measures 15 inches. Using the STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) questionnaire, which result fits her?
opts: A score of 2 misses the body mass index item: 37 kg/m2 is more than 35, so B is a yes. Tell: counting it gives 3, and that same body mass index, with her 2 yes answers to the first 4 questions, lifts her to high risk.

Her total of 3 is right, but 2 or more yes answers to the first 4 questions plus a body mass index above 35 is a separate high-risk rule. Tell: the 3-to-4 band applies only when none of the add-on rules is met, and she meets the body mass index one.

Correct. Snoring 0 + tired 1 + observed apnea 1 + pressure 0 + body mass index 37 (more than 35) 1 + age 46 0 + neck 15 inches 0 + female 0 = 3. By count that is intermediate, but yes to 2 or more of the first 4 questions plus a body mass index above 35 is a high-risk rule, so she is high risk.

A score of 4 adds a yes she does not have, such as snoring or neck size: she does not snore loudly, and her 15-inch collar is under 16 inches. Tell: her total is 3, and the risk group still rises to high through the body mass index rule.

set1.q: A 48-year-old man has loud, habitual snoring, unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches and nocturia. His wife has seen him stop breathing and wake gasping. His blood pressure is poorly controlled on two medicines. His neck circumference is 18 inches, and his posterior oropharynx is crowded. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome needs obesity (body mass index above 30) plus awake hypoventilation, an arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg, with other causes excluded. Tell: nothing here shows awake hypercapnia; his findings are those of an airway that obstructs at night.

Narcolepsy is listed with the other causes of daytime sleepiness in the differential. Tell: it does not explain witnessed apneas, gasping awakenings and loud snoring, which are events of an airway obstructing during sleep.

Correct. Loud habitual snoring, witnessed apneas, awakening with gasping, unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches, nocturia and poorly controlled hypertension are its history findings, and a large neck and a crowded posterior oropharynx are its examination findings. Narrowing of the upper airway by soft tissue or structure causes it.

Central sleep apnea sounds very similar, with insomnia, frequent awakenings and daytime sleepiness, but snoring is less common and it clusters with heart failure, stroke, opioids or high altitude. Tell: loud habitual snoring and a crowded oropharynx point to an obstructed airway.

set1.q: A 41-year-old woman has daytime sleepiness, and her partner reports habitual snoring and pauses in her breathing. Her polysomnogram shows 8 predominantly obstructive respiratory events per hour, and her symptoms are not explained by another condition, a medication or a substance. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: Central sleep apnea shows repetitive apneas in the absence of thoracic-abdominal excursion, airflow stopping because effort stops. Tell: her events are predominantly obstructive, the defining feature of obstructive sleep apnea.
Indeterminate until a home kit is done

A home kit will not always diagnose mild disease and adds nothing after a polysomnogram has answered the question. Tell: her result already meets the criterion of 5 or more events per hour with symptoms.

Correct. The diagnosis is confirmed with 5 or more predominantly obstructive events per hour plus a symptom such as sleepiness, or habitual snoring and breathing interruptions noted by a bed partner, when no other condition, medication or substance explains them. She has 8 events and those symptoms.
Not diagnostic until 15 events per hour
15 or more predominantly obstructive events per hour confirm the diagnosis without any symptom. Tell: she has symptoms, so the lower threshold of 5 events per hour applies, and her 8 events meet it.

set1.q: A 44-year-old man with obstructive sleep apnea has respiratory events on polysomnogram that occur when he sleeps on his back and not when he lies on his side. He wants a measure to add to his care. Which therapy targets this pattern?
opts: Nasal steroids treat nasal congestion and inflammation from allergic rhinitis in patients with obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: he has no nasal symptoms; his events depend on his body position.

Palatal implants are for mild obstructive sleep apnea when continuous positive airway pressure cannot be tolerated. Tell: nothing says he cannot tolerate pressure therapy, and his events are tied to position.

Tracheostomy is a cure because it bypasses the site of upper airway obstruction, but it is a surgical airway. Tell: his events depend on body position, which a sleep belt or shirt addresses without surgery.

Correct. Positional therapy fits when events occur in the supine position: a sleep belt or sleep shirt keeps him lying on his side. His events are confined to back-sleeping, the exact pattern it addresses.

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman with a body mass index of 42 kg/m2 has obesity hypoventilation syndrome, confirmed by exclusion. Her husband has witnessed few apneas, and polysomnography with continuous carbon dioxide monitoring shows sleep-related hypoventilation. Which first-line treatment fits her?
opts: Tracheostomy with nocturnal ventilation is very effective, but it is second line, for patients who fail or do not tolerate first-line therapy. Tell: she is just starting treatment and has failed nothing.

Bariatric surgery for weight loss may be helpful, but it sits in second line, after first-line therapy fails or is not tolerated. Tell: first line is a weight loss program plus positive airway pressure.
Weight loss plus bilevel positive airway pressure

Correct. First-line therapy for obesity hypoventilation syndrome is a weight loss program with positive airway pressure, and the device follows the overlap: with sleep-related hypoventilation it is bilevel positive airway pressure. Her few witnessed apneas, older age and female sex fit that 10% subgroup.
Weight loss plus continuous positive airway pressure

Continuous positive airway pressure is the first-line device when obesity hypoventilation coexists with obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: her study shows sleep-related hypoventilation with few witnessed apneas, which calls for bilevel pressure.

set1.q: A 55-year-old man started continuous positive airway pressure for obstructive sleep apnea 2 months ago. A repeat polysomnogram on the device shows repetitive apneas in the absence of thoracic-abdominal excursion. Which complication of his therapy has developed?
opts: Sleep-related hypoventilation is the third category of sleep-disordered breathing and accompanies about 10% of obesity hypoventilation syndrome, with fewer witnessed apneas. Tell: his study shows repetitive apneas without effort, the central apnea pattern.

Correct. Patients using continuous positive airway pressure are listed among those at risk for central sleep apnea. Repetitive apneas in the absence of thoracic-abdominal excursion mean airflow stops because effort stops, the polysomnogram finding of central apnea.

Residual obstructive apneas would show continued respiratory effort, the chest and abdomen moving against a collapsed airway. Tell: absent thoracic-abdominal excursion means absent effort, which is the central pattern.
ruled out by a stated finding

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is awake hypoventilation, an arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg in an obese patient with other causes excluded. Tell: his finding is a sleep event pattern of apneas without effort, not awake hypercapnia.

set1.q: A 79-year-old man with untreated obstructive sleep apnea has daytime drowsiness and nocturia. His daughter asks whether treatment is worthwhile at his age. What is accurate?
opts: Nocturia is unrelated to his apnea
Nocturia is a listed symptom of obstructive sleep apnea, and in the elderly it persists and improves with continuous positive airway pressure. Tell: both of his complaints trace back to the apnea.

Correct. Mortality from obstructive sleep apnea is lower in the elderly because they compensate, but they still have drowsiness and nocturia, and both improve with continuous positive airway pressure. Treating him targets the symptoms that affect his daily life.

Lower mortality in the elderly does not make treatment pointless: drowsiness and nocturia persist and improve with continuous positive airway pressure. Tell: the benefit at his age is relief of those symptoms.
His apnea mortality exceeds a younger man's
Mortality from obstructive sleep apnea is less in the elderly, because older patients compensate. Tell: the problem at his age is persistent drowsiness and nocturia, not a higher death rate.

set1.q: A 54-year-old man with a body mass index of 39 kg/m2 has loud snoring and daytime sleepiness. His awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure is 43 mm Hg (normal 35-45), and no other cause of hypoventilation has been found. How do his results measure against the criteria for obesity hypoventilation syndrome?
opts: Not met: carbon dioxide not above 45

Correct. The diagnosis needs all three: obesity (body mass index above 30), awake alveolar hypoventilation with an arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg, and exclusion of other causes. His body mass index of 39 qualifies, but 43 mm Hg is not above 45, so awake hypoventilation is not shown.
Met: obesity with snoring is enough

Snoring is an obstructive sleep apnea symptom found in about 90% of patients with the syndrome, but symptoms are not specific. Tell: the diagnosis turns on awake hypercapnia above 45 mm Hg, and his 43 falls short.
Met: his body mass index exceeds 35

The obesity criterion is a body mass index above 30, which his 39 meets, but obesity alone does not make the diagnosis. Tell: 35 is the screening questionnaire's body mass index item; what is missing here is a carbon dioxide above 45 mm Hg.
Not met: body mass index is too low
His body mass index of 39 is above the cut-off of 30, so the obesity criterion is met. Tell: the criterion he misses is awake hypoventilation, since 43 mm Hg is not above 45.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man with heart failure reports insomnia, frequent awakenings and nocturnal dyspnea. His wife says he rarely snores, and his breathing at night shows Cheyne-Stokes breathing (hyperventilation alternating with apnea). What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Heart failure is a risk factor for central sleep apnea, especially through Cheyne-Stokes breathing, hyperventilation alternating with apnea from increased sensitivity to carbon dioxide and a prolonged circulation delay to the carotid chemoreceptors. Insomnia, awakenings and nocturnal dyspnea fit, and snoring is less common than in obstructive apnea.

Obstructive sleep apnea brings loud, habitual snoring, and its airway collapses while the patient keeps trying to breathe. Tell: rare snoring with hyperventilation alternating with apnea in a man with heart failure points to a central cause, the brainstem signal failing.

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome needs obesity (body mass index above 30) and awake hypercapnia above 45 mm Hg with other causes excluded. Tell: nothing here shows obesity or awake hypercapnia; his pattern is the heart failure breathing of central apnea.

Panic attacks are on the differential for nighttime awakenings in suspected sleep apnea. Tell: they do not explain a sleeping pattern of hyperventilation alternating with apnea in a patient with heart failure, the risk factor tied to central apnea.

Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease
set1.q: A 51-year-old woman with untreated obstructive sleep apnea has a fasting glucose of 118 mg/dL (normal 70-99) and triglycerides of 210 mg/dL (normal below 150). Which consequence of her sleep disorder do these results reflect?
opts: Correct. Patients with obstructive sleep apnea have increased prevalence of insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and diabetes complications, and the disease is independently associated with increased glucose and triglyceride levels. It may also worsen cardiovascular risk in metabolic syndrome.

Hypothyroidism is a concomitant condition that raises the risk of obstructive sleep apnea, checked with thyroid-stimulating hormone when suspected; it is not a listed consequence. Tell: raised glucose and triglycerides are metabolic effects of the apnea itself.

Untreated obstructive sleep apnea increases cortisol; it does not cause a deficiency. Tell: the listed endocrine changes are increased C-reactive protein, cortisol and amyloid with decreased growth hormone and prolactin.

Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is 2 to 3 times more prevalent in obstructive sleep apnea, but it is a liver condition. Tell: high glucose and triglycerides point to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.

set1.q: A 52-year-old man's polysomnogram shows repeated events in which thermistor airflow falls by 90% or more for 15 seconds while chest and abdominal respiratory effort continue. How is each event classified?
opts: A hypopnea is slowed, shallow, restricted breathing in repeated episodes of 10 seconds or longer, short of a near-total stop. Tell: a fall in airflow of 90% or more is near or total cessation of breathing, which defines an apnea.

Correct. An apnea is a 90% or greater fall in airflow on the thermistor lasting at least 10 seconds, and when airflow stops but respiratory effort continues, the apnea is obstructive. The airway collapses while the patient still tries to breathe, the event pattern of obstructive sleep apnea.

A central apnea has no airflow and no respiratory effort, because the brainstem stops sending the signal to breathe. Tell: his chest and abdomen keep moving throughout each event, so effort is present and the event is not central.
ruled out by a stated finding

A mixed apnea opens with no respiratory effort, and effort resumes only during the latter part of the event. Tell: his effort is present from the start of each event to its end, which is the obstructive pattern rather than the mixed one.

set1.q: A 47-year-old man has obstructive sleep apnea newly confirmed on polysomnogram, with daytime sleepiness and hypertension. Which treatment is the most effective option for him?
opts: A nasal expiratory resistance device uses the patient's own breathing to produce expiratory positive airway pressure, an alternative device. Tell: the option named most effective is continuous positive airway pressure.

Stimulants such as modafinil target sleepiness, carry headaches, anxiety and many drug interactions, and need caution in cardiovascular conditions. Tell: a stimulant treats a symptom, while continuous positive airway pressure treats the obstruction and is the most effective option.

An oral appliance is one of the non-pharmacologic options, but it is not effective in severe obstructive sleep apnea or in patients without teeth. Tell: the treatment named most effective is continuous positive airway pressure.

Correct. Continuous positive airway pressure is the most effective non-pharmacologic treatment for obstructive sleep apnea. It also improves consequences of untreated disease, such as reflux, raised proinflammatory cytokines and, in the elderly, drowsiness and nocturia.

set1.q: A 52-year-old woman with untreated obstructive sleep apnea has nightly heartburn and symptoms of laryngopharyngeal reflux. Which treatment of her sleep apnea is expected to improve her reflux?
opts: Positional therapy with a sleep belt

Positional therapy keeps the patient on her side and suits events that occur when supine. Tell: nothing ties her apnea to position, and the treatment shown to improve this reflux is continuous positive airway pressure.

Nasal steroids treat congestion and inflammation from allergic rhinitis in patients with obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: her complaint is reflux, which improves with continuous positive airway pressure.

Correct. 75 to 100% of patients with untreated obstructive sleep apnea have gastroesophageal reflux disease or laryngopharyngeal reflux, driven by decreased intrathoracic pressure, and the reflux improves with continuous positive airway pressure. Treating her apnea treats a cause of her reflux.

A nasal expiratory resistance device uses her own breathing to produce expiratory pressure, an alternative device. Tell: the reflux of untreated sleep apnea is reported to improve with continuous positive airway pressure.

set1.q: A 57-year-old woman has a body mass index of 29 kg/m2, daytime sleepiness and an awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure of 50 mm Hg (normal 35-45). How do her results measure against the criteria for obesity hypoventilation syndrome?
opts: Not met: body mass index not above 30

Correct. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome requires obesity (body mass index above 30), awake hypoventilation with an arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg, and exclusion of alternative causes. Her carbon dioxide of 50 qualifies, but a body mass index of 29 is not above 30, so the diagnosis cannot be made.
Awake hypercapnia is one criterion, and her 50 mm Hg meets it, but the diagnosis also needs obesity, a body mass index above 30. Tell: her 29 falls just short of the obesity criterion.
The syndrome is awake hypoventilation in an obese individual, so hypercapnia without obesity does not define it. Tell: three criteria are needed, and her body mass index of 29 fails the obesity one.
Not met: carbon dioxide is too low
Her arterial carbon dioxide pressure of 50 mm Hg is above the cut-off of 45, so that criterion is met. Tell: the criterion she fails is obesity, with a body mass index of 29 not above 30.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man with a body mass index of 37 kg/m2 has an awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure of 51 mm Hg (normal 35-45). He has not yet had a chest radiograph, pulmonary function tests, thyroid function tests or a toxicology screen. What must happen before obesity hypoventilation syndrome can be diagnosed?
opts: About 90% of patients have coexisting obstructive sleep apnea symptoms, but obese individuals are screened with or without it, and it is not one of the three criteria. Tell: the missing criterion is exclusion of other causes.
Confirm a body mass index above 35

The obesity criterion for this diagnosis is a body mass index above 30, and his 37 already meets it. Tell: 35 is the screening questionnaire's body mass index item; what he lacks is exclusion of other causes.

Bilevel positive airway pressure is first-line therapy, with weight loss, for the syndrome with sleep-related hypoventilation, once it is diagnosed. Tell: his diagnosis is not yet established, because other causes have not been excluded.

Correct. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion: obesity (body mass index above 30) and awake hypercapnia (arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg) must be joined by exclusion of alternative causes of hypercapnia and hypoventilation. The workup includes a chest radiograph, pulmonary function tests, thyroid function tests and a toxicology screen.

set1.q: A 46-year-old man with moderate obstructive sleep apnea cannot tolerate continuous positive airway pressure despite several mask changes. Which option is described for his severity and his intolerance of the device?
opts: Modafinil is a stimulant for sleepiness, with headaches, anxiety and many drug interactions. Tell: no severity or device-intolerance indication is attached to it; radiofrequency ablation carries exactly his two.

Correct. Radiofrequency ablation is used in patients with mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnea who cannot tolerate continuous positive airway pressure. His disease is moderate and he cannot tolerate the device, which matches both conditions.

Palatal implants are used in mild obstructive sleep apnea when continuous positive airway pressure cannot be tolerated. Tell: his disease is moderate, beyond the mild range the implants cover; radiofrequency ablation reaches mild to moderate.

Adaptive servo-ventilation is considered for central sleep apnea after continuous positive airway pressure fails, and it is itself a positive airway pressure therapy. Tell: his disease is obstructive, and his problem is tolerating pressure therapy.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man with loud snoring, witnessed apneas and daytime sleepiness is seen for evaluation before elective surgery. He has never been tested for sleep apnea. Which property makes the STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) questionnaire suited to this visit?
opts: Correct. The questionnaire has been used as a preoperative evaluation tool for people without a known diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea who may be at risk for perioperative complications, and it has the highest sensitivity among the questionnaires. A highly symptomatic patient in a high-risk setting is where it has value.

The questionnaire is singled out for the highest sensitivity among the questionnaires, the property that suits catching at-risk patients before surgery. Tell: its strength is not missing people at risk, which is sensitivity, not specificity.
It confirms the diagnosis before surgery

A questionnaire estimates risk; obstructive sleep apnea is confirmed on a polysomnogram, with 5 or more obstructive events per hour plus symptoms, or 15 or more. Tell: the score places him in a risk group and does not replace the sleep study.

Severity is measured during a sleep study: a split-night polysomnogram records the first 2 hours of sleep to determine severity. Tell: the questionnaire gives a low, intermediate or high risk of having the disease, not a grade of disease he has.

set1.q: A 59-year-old woman with a neuromuscular disease causing generalized weakness has snoring and morning headaches. Her awake room-air oxygen saturation is 92% (normal 95-100%). Which study should evaluate her for sleep-disordered breathing?
opts: Correct. Neuromuscular weakness and awake hypoventilation or hypoxemia are both conditions in which a polysomnogram is used instead of an at-home kit. Her room-air saturation of 92% is below normal, and a polysomnogram can also find sleep disorders other than obstructive sleep apnea.

At-home kits are set aside in neuromuscular weakness and in awake hypoventilation or hypoxemia. Tell: she has both, so a home kit is the wrong study even though her snoring and headaches suggest obstructive sleep apnea.
ruled out by a stated finding

Waiting leaves her symptoms and low awake saturation unexplained, while the diagnosis of sleep-disordered breathing rests on a sleep study. Tell: her weakness and hypoxemia call for a polysomnogram now.
A positive airway pressure titration is used when the diagnosis is already known, to set the device pressure. Tell: she has no diagnosis yet; her first study must be a diagnostic polysomnogram.

set1.q: A 47-year-old man's polysomnogram shows repeated episodes, each 10 seconds or longer, of slowed, shallow, restricted breathing. Airflow is reduced but does not fall by 90%. How are these episodes classified?
opts: An obstructive apnea is a fall in airflow of 90% or more for at least 10 seconds with continued respiratory effort. Tell: his airflow stays above that threshold, so the episodes are hypopneas whatever the effort channel shows.

A central apnea has no airflow and no respiratory effort, because the brainstem stops signaling. Tell: he keeps breathing, slowly and shallowly, so neither airflow nor effort has stopped during these episodes.
ruled out by a stated finding
A mixed apnea has no airflow, with effort absent at first and resuming during the latter part of the event. Tell: his airflow is reduced, not absent, so there is no apnea here to classify as mixed.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A hypopnea is slowed, shallow, restricted breathing that occurs repeatedly during sleep in episodes of 10 seconds or longer. An apnea needs a fall in airflow of 90% or more for at least 10 seconds, which his episodes do not reach, so these are hypopneas.

set1.q: A 50-year-old woman's baseline sleep recording shows mild to moderate sleep-disordered breathing. Her clinician wants to know how severe it is in different stages of sleep and in different sleep positions. Which study fits?
opts: Correct. The all-night polysomnogram is performed when sleep-disordered breathing is mild to moderate during the baseline, and it helps determine severity in different stages of sleep and in different sleep positions, the exact question her clinician is asking.

A split-night study records the first 2 hours to set severity, then switches to continuous positive airway pressure titration when obstructive sleep apnea is significant. Tell: her baseline disease is mild to moderate, which calls for the whole night of recording.

At-home kits will not always diagnose mild obstructive sleep apnea and assess no other sleep disorder. Tell: her disease is mild to moderate and the question is severity by stage and position, which a polysomnogram answers.
ruled out by a stated finding

A positive airway pressure titration sets the device pressure when the diagnosis is already known. Tell: her clinician wants severity across stages and positions, a diagnostic question for the all-night recording.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man with obstructive sleep apnea has not been helped by continuous positive airway pressure or an oral appliance. He asks which operation would be a cure. Which procedure is described as a cure for obstructive sleep apnea?
opts: Palatal implants are an option in mild obstructive sleep apnea for patients who cannot tolerate continuous positive airway pressure. Tell: they treat mild disease; the cure comes from bypassing the upper airway obstruction.

Radiofrequency ablation is used in mild to moderate disease when continuous positive airway pressure cannot be tolerated. Tell: it is a treatment option; tracheostomy, which bypasses the obstruction, is the one called a cure.

Correct. Tracheostomy is a cure for obstructive sleep apnea because the site of upper airway obstruction is bypassed. Breathing no longer depends on the narrowed upper airway that collapses during sleep.

Bariatric surgery for weight loss may be helpful in obstructive sleep apnea, a weaker claim than a cure. Tell: the procedure called a cure is the one that bypasses the site of obstruction, tracheostomy.

set1.q: A 52-year-old woman with loud snoring and fatigue has an 8-hour polysomnogram that records 40 apneas, 32 hypopneas and 40 respiratory effort-related arousals. What is her respiratory disturbance index?
opts: 4 is the hypopneas alone, 32 / 8. Tell: the respiratory disturbance index counts apneas, hypopneas and respiratory effort-related arousals together, which gives 112 / 8 = 14.
5 is a single event type over the night, 40 / 8, either the apneas or the arousals. Tell: this index sums all three event types before dividing by the 8 hours of sleep, giving 14.
9 is the apnea-hypopnea index, (40 + 32) / 8, which leaves out the arousals. Tell: the respiratory disturbance index adds the 40 respiratory effort-related arousals, (40 + 32 + 40) / 8 = 14.

Correct. The respiratory disturbance index is (apneas + hypopneas + respiratory effort-related arousals) divided by total sleep time in hours: (40 + 32 + 40) / 8 = 112 / 8 = 14 events per hour. The arousals are obstructive airflow reductions that are neither apneas nor hypopneas.

set1.q: A 50-year-old woman with a body mass index of 41 kg/m2 and obstructive sleep apnea is being evaluated, and her clinician's suspicion of obesity hypoventilation syndrome is low to moderate. Her serum bicarbonate is 31 mEq/L (normal 22-29). What is the next step?
opts: Repeating the bicarbonate delays the step its result already triggers: above 27, the chance of the syndrome is higher and an arterial blood gas is needed. Tell: her 31 mEq/L is already above 27.

A home kit assesses obstructive sleep apnea, which she already has, and is set aside when awake hypoventilation is a concern. Tell: the missing measurement is her awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure, which comes from a blood gas.

A raised bicarbonate is a screening clue, not a criterion; the diagnosis needs an awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg and exclusion of other causes. Tell: the bicarbonate decides who gets the blood gas.

Correct. When suspicion is low to moderate, a serum bicarbonate above 27 means a higher chance of obesity hypoventilation syndrome and the need for an arterial blood gas. Her 31 mEq/L crosses that line, and the gas measures the awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure the diagnosis requires (above 45 mm Hg).

set1.q: A 34-year-old man on a mountain trek at high altitude wakes frequently at night. His tent partner notices that his breathing speeds up and then stops, over and over, without snoring. He has no heart failure and takes no medications. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Nocturnal asthma is on the differential for nighttime breathing complaints. Tell: the cycle of hyperventilation alternating with apnea, at high altitude, matches both the risk factor and the mechanism of central sleep apnea.

Correct. High altitude is a risk factor for central sleep apnea, in which increased sensitivity to carbon dioxide produces an unstable pattern of hyperventilation alternating with apnea. Frequent awakenings without snoring fit, since snoring is less common than in obstructive sleep apnea.

Obstructive sleep apnea comes from upper airway narrowing and usually brings loud, habitual snoring. Tell: a repeating cycle of fast breathing and then no breathing, at altitude and without snoring, is the central pattern.

Panic attacks are on the differential for nighttime awakenings. Tell: a repeating cycle of hyperventilation and apnea during sleep at high altitude is the breathing pattern of central apnea, not an anxiety episode.

set2.q: A 55-year-old man is having a split-night polysomnogram. The first 2 hours of sleep show significant obstructive sleep apnea. What happens during the rest of the night?
opts: Bilevel positive airway pressure is the choice for obesity hypoventilation syndrome with sleep-related hypoventilation. Tell: the split-night protocol titrates continuous positive airway pressure once significant obstructive apnea is seen.

Adaptive servo-ventilation is considered for central sleep apnea when continuous positive airway pressure fails. Tell: his first 2 hours show obstructive apnea and nothing has failed yet; the second half titrates continuous pressure.

Recording the whole night untreated is the all-night polysomnogram, performed when baseline sleep-disordered breathing is mild to moderate. Tell: his first 2 hours already show significant disease, which switches the night to titration.

Correct. In a split-night polysomnogram the first 2 hours of sleep are recorded to determine severity, and if obstructive sleep apnea is significant, the rest of the night is a continuous positive airway pressure titration that finds the exact pressure needed to keep the airway open.

Obstructive sleep apnea b. Central sleep apnea c. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (also known as Pickwickian Syndrome)
set2.q: A 64-year-old woman's polysomnogram shows events with no airflow. In each, there is no respiratory effort during the first part of the event, and effort resumes during the latter part while airflow is still absent. How are these events classified?
opts: An obstructive apnea has no airflow with continued respiratory effort throughout, the airway collapsing while the patient tries to breathe. Tell: her events open with no effort at all, which an obstructive event does not show.
ruled out by a stated finding

A central apnea has no airflow and no respiratory effort for the whole event. Tell: effort comes back during the latter part of each of her events, so the event does not stay central from start to finish.
ruled out by a stated finding

A hypopnea is slowed, shallow, restricted breathing in repeated episodes of 10 seconds or longer, with airflow reduced rather than absent. Tell: her airflow is absent, so these are apneas, and the effort pattern makes them mixed.

Correct. A mixed apnea has no airflow, with a lack of respiratory effort during the first part of the event and resumption of effort during the latter part. Her events begin like central apneas and end like obstructive ones, which is exactly the mixed pattern.

set2.q: A 76-year-old man with moderate obstructive sleep apnea has no teeth and wears full dentures. He cannot tolerate his continuous positive airway pressure mask and asks about a mouthpiece instead. Which option should be avoided?
opts: A nasal expiratory resistance device uses his own breathing to produce expiratory positive airway pressure and does not depend on teeth. Tell: the option tied to having teeth is the oral appliance.

Positional therapy with a sleep belt or sleep shirt keeps the patient on his side and fits events that occur when supine. Tell: missing teeth do not limit it; the oral appliance is the option that needs them.

Correct. An oral appliance is not effective in patients who have no teeth (or in severe obstructive sleep apnea). He is edentulous, so the mouthpiece he asks about is the option to avoid, even though he cannot tolerate his mask.

Radiofrequency ablation is used in mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnea when continuous positive airway pressure cannot be tolerated, which describes him. Tell: his lack of teeth limits the oral appliance, not this procedure.

set2.q: A 56-year-old woman with a body mass index of 44 kg/m2 has daytime hypersomnolence, loud snoring and dyspnea on exertion. Awake on room air, her arterial carbon dioxide pressure is 54 mm Hg (normal 35-45). Her chest radiograph, thyroid function tests, pulmonary function tests and toxicology screen show no other cause of hypoventilation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Narcolepsy is listed with the other causes of daytime sleepiness. Tell: it does not explain an awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg, which with a body mass index above 30 points to obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

Correct. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion made when obesity (body mass index above 30) and awake alveolar hypoventilation (arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg) are present and alternative causes of hypercapnia are excluded. Her 44 kg/m2, 54 mm Hg and negative workup meet all three.

Her snoring and hypersomnolence fit obstructive sleep apnea, which coexists in about 90% of these patients, but it does not account for awake hypercapnia of 54 mm Hg. Tell: awake carbon dioxide above 45 in an obese patient, other causes excluded, defines obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

Central sleep apnea is a pattern of apneas without respiratory effort during sleep, tied to heart failure, stroke, opioids or altitude. Tell: none of those is described for her, and her defining finding is awake hypercapnia with obesity.

Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease
set2.q: A 59-year-old man with untreated obstructive sleep apnea declines treatment and asks how the condition affects his heart. Which risk can be raised as much as 6 times in untreated disease?
opts: The 3 to 6 times risk of sudden cardiac death in untreated disease is stated for the night, during sleep, when the obstructive events happen. Tell: the figure is tied to nighttime, not to exercise.

Untreated obstructive sleep apnea triples the risk of hypertension (3 times), short of 6 times. Tell: the figure that reaches 6 times, 3 to 6, belongs to sudden cardiac death, and specifically to death at night.

Driving accidents are 2.5 times more frequent in untreated disease, because daytime sleepiness increases motor vehicle crashes. Tell: that figure is lower and is not a heart risk; 3 to 6 times is sudden cardiac death at night.

Correct. Untreated obstructive sleep apnea carries a 3- to 6-fold risk of sudden cardiac death at night, alongside high mortality from heart failure. The timing is the point: the excess risk falls during sleep, when the apneas occur.

set2.q: A 60-year-old man with untreated obstructive sleep apnea has trouble falling asleep and asks for a sleeping pill. Which option should be avoided?
opts: Positional therapy with a sleep shirt

Positional therapy with a sleep belt or sleep shirt keeps the patient on his side when events occur supine, a non-pharmacologic option. Tell: it carries no warning; sedatives and alcohol are the ones to avoid.

Correct. Use of alcohol or sedatives is a risk factor for obstructive sleep apnea, and the risk modification is to avoid alcohol and other sedatives. A sedative sleeping pill would add a risk factor to his untreated apnea.
Diet and exercise for weight loss
Diet and exercise for weight loss is a named risk modification for obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: it is advice to give him; the item on the avoid list is sedatives, along with alcohol.

Referral to a sleep physician, with proper counseling, is part of patient education for obstructive sleep apnea. Tell: this is part of his care, not something to avoid; sedatives are what he should stay away from.

Obstructive sleep apnea b. Central sleep apnea c. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (also known as Pickwickian Syndrome)
set2.q: A 60-year-old man has central sleep apnea after a stroke. His heart function is normal, he takes no opioids and he lives at sea level. A trial of continuous positive airway pressure has failed. What is the next therapy to consider?
opts: Correct. In central sleep apnea, continuous positive airway pressure is considered first, and if it fails, adaptive servo-ventilation is next: it monitors breathing patterns in real time and delivers and adjusts pressure as needed. With normal heart function he lacks the reduced ejection fraction that makes it unsafe.

Reducing opioids is the cause-directed step when the patient takes opioid medications. Tell: he takes none, so there is no opioid to reduce; his next step follows the failed trial of continuous pressure.
ruled out by a stated finding

Autotitrating positive airway pressure is an obstructive sleep apnea option for patients without significant comorbid conditions. Tell: the step named after continuous pressure fails in central apnea is adaptive servo-ventilation.

Bilevel positive airway pressure is first-line, with weight loss, for obesity hypoventilation syndrome with sleep-related hypoventilation. Tell: central sleep apnea that fails continuous pressure moves to adaptive servo-ventilation.

Obstructive sleep apnea b. Central sleep apnea c. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (also known as Pickwickian Syndrome)
set2.q: A 47-year-old man with a body mass index of 38 kg/m2 has obstructive sleep apnea. Which additional finding, with no other cause found for it, should prompt screening for obesity hypoventilation syndrome?
opts: Correct. Obese individuals, with or without obstructive sleep apnea, are screened when they have an unexplained awake room-air oxygen saturation of 94% or less or an overnight lowest under 80%, unexplained exertional dyspnea, signs of pulmonary hypertension or right heart failure, facial plethora or a raised bicarbonate. 93% awake qualifies.
The overnight trigger is a lowest saturation under 80%, and 86% does not reach it. Tell: the awake trigger is 94% or less on room air, which is why an awake reading of 93% qualifies.
A serum bicarbonate in the normal range
A raised bicarbonate prompts screening, and above 27 it calls for an arterial blood gas. Tell: a value in the normal range is not a trigger; an awake saturation of 94% or less is.

Loud snoring and witnessed apneas are obstructive sleep apnea symptoms, which he already has, and about 90% of patients with the syndrome share them. Tell: screening is prompted by the added features, such as an awake saturation of 94% or less.

set2.q: A 35-year-old woman snores loudly. She feels rested during the day, no one has seen her stop breathing, and she is not treated for high blood pressure. Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2 and her neck (shirt collar) measures 14 inches. Using the STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) questionnaire, which result fits her?
opts: A score of 1 leaves out her body mass index: 36 kg/m2 is more than 35, so the B item is a yes. Tell: her two yes answers are snoring and body mass index, which still sit in the 0-to-2 band.

Correct. Snoring 1 + tired 0 + observed 0 + pressure 0 + body mass index 36 (more than 35) 1 + age 35 0 + neck 14 inches 0 + female 0 = 2, the low-risk band (0 to 2). The body mass index rule needs 2 or more yes answers to the first 4 questions, and she has 1, so she stays low risk.

The body mass index rule moves a patient to high risk only with yes to 2 or more of the first 4 questions (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure). Tell: snoring is her single yes among the first 4 questions, so the rule is not met and her total of 2 stays low risk.

A score of 3 adds a yes she does not have: she feels rested, has no observed apneas, no treated pressure, is under 50 and has a 14-inch collar. Tell: her total is 2, snoring plus body mass index above 35.

set2.q: A 71-year-old man had a stroke last year. His wife reports loud snoring and pauses in his breathing during sleep, and a home sleep apnea kit has been ordered. What is the best next step?
opts: Change the order to a polysomnogram

Correct. Stroke is one of the conditions in which a polysomnogram is used instead of an at-home kit. Stroke is also a risk factor for central sleep apnea, and at-home testing assesses obstructive sleep apnea and is not sufficient for central apnea, so the order should change.
Proceed with the home kit as ordered

A home kit can serve uncomplicated suspected obstructive sleep apnea, but stroke is listed among the conditions that call for a polysomnogram. Tell: his stroke, not his snoring, decides the type of study.
ruled out by a stated finding

A home kit assesses only obstructive sleep apnea, a diagnostic job that is already done for him. Tell: with the diagnosis known, the open task is finding the exact air pressure, which is the job of a titration study.

Adaptive servo-ventilation is the usual step after continuous positive airway pressure fails, but it is not used for every patient, especially in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: with poor left ventricular function, reducing preload can decrease cardiac output. Cheyne-Stokes breathing can also be protective.

Continuous positive airway pressure is considered first in central sleep apnea, and no reduced-ejection-fraction warning is attached to it. Tell: the safety warning tied to poor left ventricular function belongs to adaptive servo-ventilation.

Optimizing heart failure therapy is the cause-directed treatment of central apnea in heart failure, and it is recommended, not avoided. Tell: the therapy that can lower his cardiac output by reducing preload is adaptive servo-ventilation.

Polysomnography is how central sleep apnea is diagnosed, and no heart failure restriction is attached to it. Tell: the hazard in reduced ejection fraction is the preload-lowering effect of adaptive servo-ventilation.

An in-laboratory polysomnogram is the study used when awake hypoventilation is present. Tell: it is recommended for him; the kit is the study to avoid.

opts: 7 is the hypopneas alone, 42 / 6, leaving out his 48 apneas. Tell: the index adds apneas and hypopneas before dividing by the hours of sleep, so (48 + 42) / 6 = 15 events per hour.

set2.q: A 56-year-old man is seen for evaluation before elective knee surgery and has no known sleep disorder. His wife says he snores loudly enough to be heard through closed doors and has seen him stop breathing during sleep. He denies daytime tiredness. He is treated for high blood pressure. His body mass index is 33 kg/m2 and his neck (shirt collar) measures 16.5 inches. What is his STOP-Bang (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure, body mass index, age, neck, gender) score?
opts: A score of 4 drops two yes answers, such as age and neck: 56 is older than 50, and a 16.5-inch collar meets the 16-inch item. Tell: he meets three of the four Bang items (age, neck, male), on top of three yes answers to the first 4 questions (snoring, observed apnea, pressure).

A score of 5 misses one yes answer, most often the neck: the questionnaire counts a collar of 16 inches / 40 cm or larger for anyone, so 16.5 inches scores 1. Tell: on the questionnaire, the neck item has a single cut-off, 16 inches, whatever the patient's sex.

Correct. Snoring 1 + tired 0 + observed apnea 1 + treated pressure 1 + body mass index 33 (not more than 35) 0 + age 56 (older than 50) 1 + neck 16.5 inches (16 or larger) 1 + male 1 = 6. A score of 5 to 8 places him in the high-risk group for obstructive sleep apnea before his surgery.

A score of 7 adds a point for body mass index, but the item asks for more than 35 kg/m2, and his 33 does not qualify. Tell: being obese is not enough for the B item; it needs a body mass index above 35, and his tiredness item is also a no.

opts: In obstructive sleep apnea the airway collapses while the patient still tries to breathe, so the chest and abdomen keep moving. Tell: absent thoracic-abdominal excursion means absent effort, the central pattern.
ruled out by a stated finding

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome requires obesity and an awake arterial carbon dioxide pressure above 45 mm Hg, other causes excluded. Tell: neither is described, and opioids plus apneas without effort point to central apnea.
Narcolepsy is listed with the other causes of daytime sleepiness. Tell: it does not explain repetitive apneas on her polysomnogram; apneas without thoracic-abdominal movement are central apneas.

Correct. Repetitive apneas in the absence of thoracic-abdominal excursion are the polysomnogram finding of central sleep apnea: airflow stops because respiratory effort stops. Opioid medications are a listed risk factor, and frequent awakenings, nonrestorative sleep and sleepiness with little snoring fit.
